title: Selective Writing – Practice Prompts
markingGuide:
MARKING GUIDE – NSW Selective High School Placement Test, Writing (practice)

You are an experienced marker for the NSW Selective High School Placement Test writing task. You are giving feedback on a practice response written by an 11-year-old in Year 6, typed in 30 minutes. Her parent will read your feedback first.

Official criteria (each examiner marks out of 25; two examiners' marks are added):
• Set A – up to 15 marks – content, form, organisation and style. Awareness of purpose and audience shown by: selecting interesting content and relevant details; using an appropriate form; organising ideas coherently, using paragraphs and a range of cohesive devices; using a deliberately chosen style, range of vocabulary and level of formality.
• Set B – up to 10 marks – using a range of sentence lengths, types and structures and correct punctuation; spelling correctly.
• A response that does not address the given topic and form is marked lower, however fluent or creative it is.
• Markers reward a title that sums up the piece, original and interesting ideas, precise vocabulary and imagery, and a complete structure that reaches a conclusion. Quality matters more than length.

Please reply in this order, in plain language, under 450 words:
1. TASK CHECK – Does it answer the topic, use the required form (e.g. newspaper report, diary entry) and suit the audience? Yes / Partly / No, with one sentence.
2. ESTIMATED MARK – Set A __/15 and Set B __/10 (total __/25), one sentence of reasoning for each. Be honest and calibrated; do not inflate. Say it is an estimate from one marker.
3. TWO STRENGTHS – quote her own words.
4. THREE IMPROVEMENTS, most important first – each with a short quote from her text and a better version she could have written.
5. ONE PARAGRAPH REWRITTEN – her weakest paragraph, improved but still in her voice and at a strong Year 6 level (not adult writing).
6. SPELLING AND PUNCTUATION – up to 8 errors as wrong → right. Write 'None found' if there are none.
7. NEXT PRACTICE – one 10-minute exercise targeting her biggest weakness.
Address points 3–7 to the student warmly and directly. End with a two-line note for the parent: the one thing to focus on before the next practice.

prompts.label: Story
prompts.title: The last bus
prompts.task: Write a story that begins with the sentence below.
prompts.start: The last bus of the night pulled away, and that was when I realised my bag was still on it.
could: who you are and what is in the bag
what you do to get it back, and who helps or gets in the way
how you feel at different moments
how the story ends – does anything change for you?

prompts.label: Letter
prompts.title: Save Fig Tree Park
prompts.context: Your local council plans to turn Fig Tree Park into a car park for the new shopping centre. The park has a playground, a big old fig tree and an open grassy area where people meet on weekends.
prompts.task: Write a letter to the mayor to persuade the council to change its plan.
could: give your strongest reasons, with examples of how people use the park
show you understand why the council wants more parking
suggest a better solution
finish politely but firmly, telling the mayor what you want them to do

prompts.label: News
prompts.title: Foam flood on Main Street
prompts.context: Early on Saturday morning, someone poured a large bottle of bubble bath into the fountain in your town square. By 9 am, a wall of foam had spread down Main Street, covering footpaths, cars and the front of several shops.
prompts.task: Write a newspaper report about this event for your local paper.
could: explain what happened, when and where
describe the effect on shops, drivers and people in town
include comments from people who were there
say what happens next – the clean-up, and whether anyone is in trouble

prompts.label: Guide
prompts.title: A visitor's guide to the beach
prompts.context: A visitor from another planet is coming to stay with your family for the summer. They have never been to a beach and know nothing about how people behave there.
prompts.task: Write a guide for the visitor about how to spend a safe and enjoyable day at an Australian beach.
could: what to bring and why
beach safety rules and what the flags and signs mean
how to behave around other people
the best things to do, and things to avoid

prompts.label: Diary
prompts.title: Principal for a day
prompts.context: Your school ran a competition, and the prize was to be principal for one day. You won.
prompts.task: Write a diary entry about your day as principal. Use the sentence below to start your diary.
prompts.start: Dear Diary, I never thought Mrs Hayes would actually hand me her keys, but at 8:30 this morning…
could: the decisions you made and why
something that went wrong, and how you handled it
how teachers and students reacted
what you learnt about being in charge

prompts.label: Review
prompts.title: Rate it!
prompts.context: A website for kids your age is asking readers to send in reviews.
prompts.task: Write a review of a book, film or game you know well, telling other readers whether it is worth their time.
could: what it is about, without giving away the ending
what is best about it, and what could be better
who would enjoy it most
a final rating out of five stars, with your reason

prompts.label: Speech
prompts.title: A later start?
prompts.context: Your school is thinking about starting the school day one hour later, at 10 am, and finishing one hour later, at 4 pm. The principal has asked students to share their views at assembly.
prompts.task: Write a speech for the school assembly that discusses both sides of the idea and then gives your own view.
could: the benefits of a later start
the problems it might cause for students and families
a fair comparison of both sides
your view, and a strong closing line for your audience
